opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and some of them are a bit counterintuitive.

The first is talent. Europe has an extraordinary pool of scientists and engineers. If you look at the people who built the foundational work in deep learning over the last decade, a lot of them came out of European schools: in France, the École Polytechnique, the École Normale Supérieure, and similar institutions in the UK, Switzerland, and Germany. Historically, many of those people left for the US because that's where the frontier labs were. What we've seen since starting the company is that if you give them a reason to stay, a frontier-level project with real ambition, a lot of them want to stay. Some want to come back. So talent density is not the constraint people assume it is.

The second is that the technology has properties that make it possible to compete without being the biggest spender in the room. When we started, our bet was that you could be much more efficient: train smaller models that perform very well, be disciplined about compute, focus on the data and the training recipe. You don't need to be the company with the largest cluster on day one to build something people want to use. Efficiency is a real competitive advantage, especially when customers care about cost, latency, and running models on their own infrastructure.

The third, which I think matters most, is that there's genuine demand for an independent alternative. AI is becoming infrastructure. It will shape how people access information, how governments operate, how companies run. Many enterprises and states, in Europe and well beyond it, don't want to depend entirely on a few providers from one country. They want control: to deploy on-premise, to customize models, to understand what's inside them. That's why we took a strong position on open weights and portability. There's a market for that, and a European company is naturally well positioned to serve it.

There's also a cultural dimension. Language models carry values and languages and a certain view of the world. Having a diversity of actors building them, not just one geography, is healthy for everyone. Europe has a lot of languages and a lot of cultures, and building for that from the start makes you better at serving a global market.

Of course there are challenges. Capital markets in Europe have historically been less deep for this kind of company, and there's regulatory complexity. But capital is global, and we've been able to raise what we needed. On regulation, we've tried to be constructive, to make sure the rules focus on applications and real risks rather than on stifling the underlying technology.

So my answer is: the talent is here, the technology rewards efficiency and not just scale, and the world wants more than a couple of options. That combination makes it possible. Now it's on us to execute.

r001.rationale: It cites European scientific and engineering talent and named schools, but does not identify mathematics education as the source of that advantage.

r002.rationale: It says many talented people want to stay in Europe when given an ambitious frontier project, and some want to return.

r003.rationale: It mentions frontier labs as a reason people historically left for the US, but does not credit established AI research labs with catalyzing European AI ecosystems.

r004.rationale: It discusses European talent and France's schools, but does not describe France's AI ecosystem as developing Bay Area-like self-reinforcing dynamics.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say is that the ingredients for building a frontier AI company are not as location-bound as people assume. What you need is a dense core of people who really understand how to train these models, access to compute, and the ability to move fast. Europe has always had the first one. If you look at where a lot of the researchers at DeepMind, OpenAI, Meta FAIR came from, a very large fraction were trained in Paris, in Zurich, in Cambridge, in Berlin. The talent was here. It was just leaving, because for a long time there was no place in Europe where you could do this kind of work at scale.

So part of our thesis with Mistral was simply that if you create that place, people come back. And that's what happened. We had people who'd been at DeepMind for years, at Meta, who wanted to come home and work on something ambitious, and before us there wasn't really an option. That's an enormous advantage that's hard to see from Silicon Valley, because from there it just looks like everyone is already in the Bay Area.

The second thing is that the market itself is global and, importantly, it's not going to be served by one or two companies. Enterprises, governments, developers want choice. They want models they can run themselves, that they can inspect, that they can adapt to their own data and their own constraints. Europe in particular has very strong feelings about sovereignty and about not being dependent on a handful of American providers for what's going to be critical infrastructure. That's a real pull. But it's not only Europe. We see the same thing in Asia, in the Middle East, in large US enterprises. Being an independent, open-weight-friendly provider is a differentiated position, and being European actually makes that story more credible, not less.

And then the third thing, honestly, is efficiency. We started with a lot less capital than the big American labs. That forced us to be very disciplined about how we use compute, about model architecture, about what we train and when. Mistral 7B and Mixtral were good examples of that: you can get a lot further with clever engineering than people expected. Constraints are annoying, but they produce good habits. I think that's turned out to be a strength rather than a handicap.

So I don't think it's surprising, or that it requires some special explanation. The talent is here, the demand is global, and the technology doesn't care about geography. What was missing was someone willing to try.

r001.rationale: The response cites European research talent and training in cities such as Paris, but does not identify mathematics education as the source of that advantage.

r002.rationale: It says researchers who had left for DeepMind or Meta wanted to come home and that people came back when Mistral created a place to work on ambitious AI in Europe.

r003.rationale: It names established labs as places where European-trained researchers worked, but does not credit those labs with catalyzing European AI ecosystems.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe France's AI ecosystem or compare its dynamics with the San Francisco Bay Area.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is talent. Europe has very strong scientific training, particularly in mathematics and computer science, and there are excellent researchers and engineers who want to build here. So the ingredients are there. The challenge is bringing them together in a company that can move quickly and compete globally from the beginning.

And AI is an opportunity to do that because the technology is changing so quickly. You can come in with a small team, make good technical choices, and build something that matters. You don’t necessarily need to inherit the distribution or the infrastructure of an incumbent to have an impact.

Of course, being European isn’t enough. You have to make products that people choose because they’re useful and competitive. That’s the ambition: to build from Europe, but for users everywhere.

r001.rationale: The response names strong European training in mathematics as part of the region’s talent advantage.

r002.rationale: It says researchers and engineers want to build in Europe, communicating a preference to stay and build there.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention established AI research labs or their role in catalyzing ecosystems.

r004.rationale: It does not describe France’s ecosystem or compare its dynamics to the San Francisco Bay Area.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s sometimes a confusion between where the technology gets built and where the talent comes from. Europe has a very strong tradition in mathematics and computer science, and a lot of the people building AI in American labs were trained here. So the talent exists. The question is whether you can bring it together with the capital and the ambition to build a global company.

And AI creates an opportunity because the technology is moving so quickly. You don’t need to reproduce every advantage that an incumbent has accumulated over twenty years. You need a strong team, good research judgment, and a way to get your models into developers’ hands. From Europe, you can serve developers and businesses everywhere. That’s the ambition: build here, but compete globally.

r001.rationale: It cites Europe’s strong tradition in mathematics and computer science and says many AI builders were trained there, linking that background to Europe’s talent advantage.

r002.rationale: It says AI talent exists in Europe, but does not say AI professionals prefer to remain there.

r003.rationale: It mentions American labs as places where European-trained people work, but does not credit established labs with catalyzing European AI ecosystems.

r004.rationale: It does not describe France’s AI ecosystem or compare its dynamics with the San Francisco Bay Area.
